Executive Summary and Statutory Evolution of the Canadian R&D Tax Landscape

The Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program constitutes the foundational pillar of federal innovation policy in Canada and operates as the single largest federal government program supporting business research and development (R&D) across the jurisdiction. Although the federal government first introduced statutory tax assistance for industrial research in 1944, the contemporary architecture of the SR&ED program was codified in 1994 under the federal Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), hereinafter the "ITA") and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945, hereinafter the "ITR"). Administered jointly by the Department of Finance Canada, which holds statutory responsibility for tax policy design and legislative drafting, and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), which executes technical eligibility reviews, financial audits, and tax assessments, the program delivers non-discretionary statutory entitlements through a dual-mechanism structure. Under the first mechanism, codified in Subsection 37(1) of the ITA, a qualifying taxpayer carrying on business in Canada is entitled to pool and immediately deduct 100% of allowable current and capital SR&ED expenditures in computing business income in the taxation year incurred, or carry the undeducted pool balance forward indefinitely to shelter future taxable income, even though such expenditures generate enduring knowledge, technology, and intangible capital assets that would otherwise require multi-year amortization. Under the second mechanism, codified in Subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the ITA, the taxpayer earns an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) ranging from a basic rate of 15% to an enhanced rate of 35% of qualified SR&ED expenditures, which either reduces Part I federal income tax otherwise payable or triggers a direct cash refund under Section 127.1 of the ITA.

During the first two decades of the twenty-first century, overall business participation in the federal SR&ED program experienced a pronounced structural contraction driven by macroeconomic shifts and legislative tightening. Aggregate business SR&ED expenditures claimed across Canada reached a historical peak of nearly $19.6 billion in 2001 before declining by 30% to $13,611,259,539 across 21,277 claiming businesses by the 2016 taxation year. Similarly, after reaching a peak participation level of approximately 27,500 claimant firms in 2009, the total number of enterprises claiming SR&ED tax credits declined in every subsequent year, falling by 23% between 2009 and 2016. This sustained contraction followed a series of fiscal restraint measures enacted in the 2012 Federal Budget, which reduced the general corporate SR&ED ITC rate from 20% to 15%, lowered the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) overhead rate from 65% (for 2012 and prior years) to 60% in 2013 and 55% for 2014 and subsequent taxation years, curtailed the ITC inclusion rate for arm's-length contract expenditures from 100% to 80%, and completely eliminated the eligibility of SR&ED capital expenditures and capital lease costs incurred after 2013.

Recognizing that the post-2012 capital exclusions, combined with the strict statutory bar preventing Canadian public corporations from accessing the enhanced 35% refundable credit and an unindexed taxable capital phase-out corridor, were constraining domestic R&D intensity and incentivizing scaling Canadian firms to migrate intellectual property (IP) offshore, the Department of Finance Canada launched a comprehensive two-phase legislative consultation on the SR&ED program in 2024. The first phase of public consultations ran from January 31, 2024, to April 15, 2024, followed by a second consultation phase announced in Budget 2024 (Fairness for Every Generation) that concluded on May 27, 2024. Through these consultations, the Department of Finance solicited stakeholder input on modernizing the statutory definition and architecture of SR&ED, improving complementarity with direct innovation programs such as the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP), streamlining administrative compliance for entrepreneurs, and establishing mechanisms to retain Canadian-developed IP within Canadian-owned and operated enterprises.

Culminating from the 2024 consultations, the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES), followed by detailed legislative proposals released by the Department of Finance in August and November 2025 and enacted through the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1 (S.C. 2026, c. 3), introduced the most expansive structural modernization of the federal SR&ED regime since 1994. Having received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, these statutory amendments double the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3 million to $6 million, increase the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10 million and $50 million to $15 million and $75 million, extend the enhanced 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, and fully restore the eligibility of SR&ED capital expenditures, capital equipment lease costs, and Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024. Furthermore, Budget 2026 reinforced this modernized statutory foundation by introducing binding upfront CRA pre-claim rulings before capital is committed—governed by a strict "1 project, 1 decision, 1 year" service standard—alongside targeted SR&ED commercialization measures and renewed clean-technology support through NRC IRAP.

body.text: Statutory Definition of SR&ED and Judicial Precedents
The Subsection 248(1) Statutory Framework

The statutory threshold governing whether industrial, scientific, or academic activity qualifies for federal and provincial R&D tax incentives in Canada is codified in Subsection 248(1) of the ITA, which absorbed the regulatory definition formerly located in Subsection 2900(1) of the ITR. Pursuant to Subsection 248(1), "scientific research and experimental development" is defined as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. The statute bifurcates qualifying investigations into three core scientific or technological branches—basic research, applied research, and experimental development—supplemented by a fourth derivative category of eligible support work.

Under Paragraph (a) of the definition in Subsection 248(1), basic research encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view, whereas Paragraph (b) defines applied research as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Paragraph (c) codifies experimental development—the branch under which the vast majority of corporate Canadian SR&ED claims are filed—as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Finally, Paragraph (d) permits a claimant to include work with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, but strictly limits the eligibility of such support activities to circumstances where the work is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of the basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.

Conversely, paragraphs (e) through (k) of the definition of SR&ED in Subsection 248(1) of the ITA explicitly enumerate excluded work—activities that are statutorily disqualified from SR&ED treatment even if they are technically demanding or performed by qualified scientists and engineers. These statutory exclusions comprise market research or sales promotion (defined in CRA policy as work that supplements advertising and personal selling, coordinating them and making them effective); quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; research in the social sciences or the humanities; prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process (including any excess production beyond what is strictly required for the SR&ED investigation); style changes; and routine data collection, noting that data collection is only eligible under Paragraph (d) when it is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of basic research, applied research, or experimental development.
Foundational and Contemporary Case Law Jurisprudence

Because the statutory architecture of Subsection 248(1) turns on qualitative scientific concepts—specifically "systematic investigation or search," "experiment or analysis," and "technological advancement"—Canadian tax jurisprudence has established the definitive legal boundaries separating eligible SR&ED from ineligible routine engineering or standard practice.
Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (1998)

The seminal judicial precedent governing SR&ED eligibility in Canada is the decision of the Tax Court of Canada in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 D.T.C. 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 1998 CarswellNat 696 (T.C.C.), authored by Judge (later Chief Justice) Donald G.H. Bowman. Tasked with evaluating whether physical hydraulic scale modelling projects constituted eligible experimental development, Judge Bowman formulated the foundational five-question judicial test that both Canadian courts and the CRA apply to determine whether a project constitutes SR&ED.

Under the first criterion of the Northwest Hydraulic framework, the court asks whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. Judge Bowman defined "routine engineering" as encompassing techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field, and famously observed that technological uncertainty is something that exists in the mind of the specialist. Where the resolution of a technical problem is not reasonably predictable using established engineering methodologies or publicly available knowledge, genuine technological uncertainty exists. Under the second criterion, the court examines whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty, which entails a five-step cognitive and operational process: observing the subject matter of the problem, formulating a clear objective, identifying and articulating the technological uncertainty, formulating a hypothesis or hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate that uncertainty, and methodically verifying those hypotheses.

The third criterion requires that the procedures adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method (or established and objective principles of the scientific method), characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement, and experiment, as well as the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses. Unstructured trial-and-error or intuitive debugging fails this third requirement. The fourth criterion asks whether the process resulted in a technological advancement, meaning an advancement in the general understanding of science or technology available to competent professionals in the field, even if the experiment ultimately proves that a specific hypothesis does not work. Finally, the fifth criterion asks whether the taxpayer kept a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results as the work progressed.
RIS-Christie Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen (1998/1999) and C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada (2001)

Shortly after Northwest Hydraulic, the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA)—the appellate court above the Tax Court of Canada—endorsed Judge Bowman's analytical framework in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen, 99 D.T.C. 5087, [1999] 1 C.T.C. 132 (F.C.A.). Evaluating the development of reusable concrete forming panels, the FCA held that repeatability is the essence of the scientific method and that documentary evidence of testing is vital to discharging the taxpayer's burden of proof, while clarifying that the absence of specific contemporaneous intent documents is an evidentiary weight consideration rather than an absolute statutory bar if credible objective evidence establishes that systematic experimentation occurred.

Subsequently, in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Her Majesty the Queen (also cited as C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada), 2001 FCA 393, 2002 D.T.C. 6740 (Docket A-601-00, judgment delivered from the bench at Toronto on December 11, 2001), a unanimous panel of the Federal Court of Appeal comprising Justices Stone, Evans, and Sexton (with Justice Sexton writing for the Court) formally codified the five criteria from Northwest Hydraulic as binding appellate law. The appellant, C.W. Agencies Inc., marketed lottery tickets worldwide by telephone and computer in multiple languages to between two and three million customers, processing up to 25,000 purchases per day, and claimed current and capital SR&ED expenditures for custom software development across its 1991 through 1995 taxation years. Upholding Tax Court Judge Bonner's dismissal of the taxpayer's appeal, the FCA reaffirmed at paragraph 17 that the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria govern the determination of SR&ED under Regulation 2900 (now Subsection 248(1) of the ITA). Because the Tax Court Judge properly weighed the competing expert testimonies and preferred the Crown's expert, who demonstrated that the multilingual lottery transaction software was built using standard software engineering practices rather than resolving a genuine computer science or technological uncertainty, the FCA dismissed the appeal with costs.
Evolution of Jurisprudence: From Jentel and Kam-Press to Manning Canning (2011–2025)

Over the two decades following C.W. Agencies, the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal have rigorously applied and refined the five Bowman criteria across traditional manufacturing, fisheries processing, electromechanical systems, and food science. In D'Eon Fisheries Ltd. / Blue Wave Seafoods Inc. v. The Queen, 2004 TCC (Dockets 2001-2140(IT)G, 2002-1248(IT)G, and 2002-1249(IT)G), Justice Miller applied Northwest Hydraulic to silver hake harvesting and surimi processing machinery adaptations across 1995–1998 claims, distinguishing commercial fishery development from systematic experimental adaptation of processing equipment. In Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 TCC (affirmed by the FCA), Justice D'Arcy synthesized Northwest Hydraulic and C.W. Agencies to dismiss a taxpayer's appeal where reliance on a narrow Statement of Agreed Facts failed to provide the trial judge with concrete evidence of technological uncertainty or systematic hypothesis formulation. Conversely, in 6379249 Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC (Docket 2012-3634), the Tax Court ruled in favour of the taxpayer on a portable printing capability project, finding that systematically testing felt materials to balance motor power consumption between static and dynamic regimes—thereby minimizing motor stalling—resolved a technological uncertainty that could not be overcome through routine engineering.

In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA (Docket A-442-19), the Federal Court of Appeal reaffirmed the binding force of Northwest Hydraulic, RIS-Christie, C.W. Agencies, and Jentel, upholding the Tax Court's dismissal of a metal stamping manufacturer's claim strictly on the third Bowman criterion. The FCA held that the taxpayer's failure to demonstrate that its shop-floor procedures accorded with established and objective principles of the scientific method—characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement, and experiment, and the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses—was fatal to its appeal.

Most recently, in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King, 2024 TCC 159 (Docket 2023-2126(IT)I; amended reasons issued January 17, 2025), Justice Bodie delivered a landmark taxpayer victory under the Tax Court's informal procedure that tempers overly rigid CRA audit interpretations. The appellant sought to develop an unpasteurized cold-pressed juice product capable of remaining shelf-stable at room temperature for at least two years; during initial trials, microbial growth released oxygen that caused the sealed cans to explode. The Minister disallowed the claim, arguing that experimenting with commercially available preservatives (potassium sorbate, sodium benzoate, and Chiber) amounted to routine food engineering. Rejecting the Crown's position, Justice Bodie relied on Chief Justice Bowman's reasoning in Northwest Hydraulic, which invokes Section 12 of the federal Interpretation Act, under which every enactment is deemed remedial and must be given "such fair, large and liberal construction and interpretation as best ensures the attainment of its objects". The Court held that achieving a two-year ambient shelf life in unpasteurized cold-pressed juice presented a genuine technological uncertainty, that the appellant's structured testing of preservative interactions satisfied the scientific method and generated a technological advancement, and—adopting Justice Jorré's statement in Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen, 2014 TCC 313, at paragraph 94, that "the existence of contemporaneous documentation, or contemporaneous documents with specific intent, is not a condition to the recognition of scientific research or experimental development"—accepted the appellant's testimony that it had kept contemporaneous records of its hypotheses, tests, and results throughout its 2020 taxation year.

body.text: Federal SR&ED Financial Mechanics, Rates, and Thresholds
The Section 37 Deduction Pool vs. The Section 127 Investment Tax Credit

The financial mechanics of the federal SR&ED program operate through two distinct but mathematically linked statutory provisions in the ITA: the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and the Section 127 Investment Tax Credit. Under Subsection 37(1) of the ITA, a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada adds allowable current SR&ED expenditures under Paragraph 37(1)(a) and, for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, allowable capital SR&ED expenditures under Paragraph 37(1)(b) into a cumulative tax pool. Rather than amortizing R&D costs over multiple years as capital or intangible assets, the Section 37 pool allows the taxpayer to deduct up to 100% of the available pool balance against business income for tax purposes in the current taxation year—reported on Line 411 of Schedule T2SCH1—or to carry forward any undeducted pool balance indefinitely to reduce taxable income in future taxation years.

Simultaneously, based on the claimant's "qualified expenditures" determined under Subsection 127(9) of the ITA, the claimant earns an SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC) that is applied to reduce Part I federal income tax otherwise payable under Subsection 127(5) or refunded in cash under Section 127.1. To the extent that a non-refundable ITC exceeds the taxpayer's Part I federal tax otherwise payable in the current year, the unused credit may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years (subject to the tax payable limits in those years) or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years.

To prevent double dipping on the same expenditure dollar, the ITA enforces strict pool-reduction rules for both federal and provincial tax incentives. Any provincial or territorial R&D tax credit or grant (such as the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit, the Québec R&D Tax Credit, or the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant) constitutes "government assistance" under Subsection 127(9) of the ITA and must be deducted directly from both the Section 37 deductible pool and qualified expenditures in the current taxation year (year t) on Lines 513 and 514 of Form T661. Conversely, any federal SR&ED ITC claimed against Part I tax or refunded in cash in taxation year t is deducted from the taxpayer's Section 37 pool in the immediately following taxation year (year t + 1) under Paragraph 37(1)(e) of the ITA (or included in income under Paragraph 12(1)(t) if the pool becomes negative), thereby subjecting the federal ITC to corporate income tax in year t + 1.
Enhanced (35%) vs. Basic (15%) ITC Rates and Refundability Rules

The federal SR&ED program utilizes a two-tier ITC rate structure that differentiates claimants by corporate status, size, and whether expenditures fall within or exceed the annual expenditure limit. The basic (general) ITC rate is 15% of qualified SR&ED expenditures and applies to large corporations, foreign-controlled Canadian subsidiaries, Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) on qualified expenditures exceeding their annual expenditure limit, sole proprietorships (individuals), partners of a partnership, and beneficiaries of trusts.

In contrast, the enhanced ITC rate of 35% applies to qualified SR&ED expenditures up to the claimant's annual expenditure limit. For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, access to the enhanced 35% rate was restricted exclusively to CCPCs up to a maximum annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000 (shared among associated CCPCs). Following the enactment of the 2024 FES and Budget 2025 legislative amendments (Royal Assent March 26, 2026), for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the maximum annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% rate is doubled to $6,000,000, and eligibility is expanded to encompass both CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs).

Refundability of earned ITCs varies according to the claimant category and whether the underlying expenditure is of a current or capital nature. For a qualifying CCPC or, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, an ECPC, ITCs earned at the 35% enhanced rate up to the annual expenditure limit are 100% refundable on current expenditures (yielding a 35% cash refund) and 40% refundable on restored capital expenditures (yielding a 14% cash refund, with the remaining 60% of the credit non-refundable). On qualified expenditures exceeding the annual expenditure limit, a CCPC that is a "qualifying corporation" under Subsection 127.1(2) of the ITA—one whose prior-year taxable income (together with that of its associated corporations) does not exceed its qualifying income limit of $500,000, reduced on a straight-line basis as prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada rises from $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 ($10,000,000 to $50,000,000 pre-reform)—earns the 15% basic ITC with 40% refundability on both current and capital expenditures, whereas CCPCs that are not qualifying corporations, ECPCs on expenditures above their expenditure limit, and all large or foreign-controlled corporations earn the 15% basic ITC on a strictly non-refundable basis. Sole proprietorships (individuals) and trusts earn the 15% basic ITC with a 40% refundability rate.

Because the taxable income test penalized profitable, high-growth firms as soon as their prior-year taxable income exceeded $500,000, Budget 2019 repealed taxable income as a factor in determining a CCPC's annual expenditure limit for taxation years ending after March 19, 2019.
Pre-December 16, 2024 CCPC Expenditure Limit Formula

For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the annual expenditure limit of a CCPC (shared across all associated CCPCs) is $3,000,000, reduced on a straight-line basis when the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC and its associated CCPCs reaches $10,000,000 and becoming nil when prior-year taxable capital reaches $50,000,000:

Expenditure limit = $3,000,000 × ($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000, where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is $10,000,000 or less, and otherwise the lesser of $40,000,000 and the amount by which that taxable capital exceeds $10,000,000
Post-December 15, 2024 CCPC and ECPC Expenditure Limit Formulas

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the maximum annual expenditure limit is increased to $6,000,000 (prorated for short taxation years and subject to specialized rules where a CCPC has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year while associated with another CCPC). The prior-year taxable capital phase-out range is expanded to begin at $15,000,000 and become nil at $75,000,000 (representing a $60,000,000 phase-out span across the associated group):

Expenditure limit = $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000, where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is $15,000,000 or less, and otherwise the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which that taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000

For an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) whose taxation year begins after December 15, 2024—or for a CCPC (or group of associated CCPCs) that elects under the amended ITA provisions to calculate its expenditure limit using the ECPC method—the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is shared among members of the consolidated group and is reduced on a straight-line basis when the corporation's (or consolidated group's) average annual revenue over the preceding three fiscal years exceeds $15,000,000, becoming nil at $75,000,000. If a CCPC group elects into this revenue-based method, it must use the total of all amounts of average annual revenue reflected in the financial statements for each corporation that is a member of the group for the taxation year in question over the preceding three fiscal years, regardless of whether those corporations were associated during the entirety of that three-year period:

Expenditure limit = $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000, where A is nil if average annual revenue is $15,000,000 or less, and otherwise the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which average annual revenue exceeds $15,000,000
Qualifying Expenditures (QREs) and Calculation Methodologies
Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method

When filing Form T661, a claimant must elect annually for each taxation year whether to compute its SR&ED expenditures using the Traditional Method, governed by Clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) of the ITA and Subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3) of the ITR, or the Proxy Method, governed by Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I) to (VI) of the ITA and Subsection 2900(4) of the ITR. Once selected on the filed Form T661 for a taxation year, the choice of method is irrevocable for that year.

Under the Proxy Method, the claimant does not specifically identify, track, or allocate overhead and other indirect SR&ED expenditures on Form T661. Instead, the claimant calculates a notional substitute amount—the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)—in Part 5 of Form T661 equal to 55% of the eligible salary base of employees directly engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (a rate that has been fixed at 55% since 2014, following reductions from 65% in 2012 and 60% in 2013). Because the PPA is strictly a notional amount included in the definition of "qualified expenditure" under Subsection 127(9) of the ITA for the purpose of earning SR&ED ITCs, neither the PPA nor the underlying overhead expenses it represents (such as office supplies, utilities, support or clerical staff wages, and general purpose office equipment or furniture) can be added to the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures. Rather, the claimant deducts its actual overhead outlays as ordinary business expenses under Subsection 9(1) of the ITA. Furthermore, to ensure that the notional PPA does not exceed the taxpayer's actual non-SR&ED business expenses, the ITR imposes an overall cap on the PPA calculated by the formula:
PPA cap = A − B − C

where A is the total of all amounts deducted in computing net income for tax purposes from the business for the year (including cost of goods sold), and B and C are specific statutory deductions identified in the ITR, including Capital Cost Allowance (CCA), the Section 37 SR&ED deduction claimed on Line 411 of Schedule T2SCH1, building rent, and interest expense.

Conversely, under the Traditional Method, the claimant foregoes the 55% PPA and instead identifies, tracks, allocates, and substantiates all actual overhead and other expenditures (reported on Line 360 of Form T661) that are directly related to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada and incremental—meaning the expenditure, or portion thereof, would not have been incurred if the prosecution of SR&ED had not occurred—as well as incremental costs for the maintenance and upkeep of SR&ED premises, facilities, or equipment under Paragraphs 2900(2)(c) and 2900(3)(b) of the ITR. Under the Traditional Method, eligible overhead and administrative SR&ED salaries are added to the Section 37 deductible pool and also earn Section 127 ITCs directly.

body.text: Salaries, Wages, and the Specified Employee Regime

Salaries and wages constitute the primary cost driver of Canadian SR&ED claims. Under the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, eligible salary or wages include gross base remuneration and the employer's share of payroll-related statutory contributions (such as Canada Pension Plan [CPP], Québec Pension Plan [QPP], Employment Insurance [EI], and provincial payroll taxes or workers' compensation premiums) paid to employees for the proportion of their time spent directly engaged in SR&ED. Determining whether an employee is "directly engaged" in the prosecution of SR&ED is a question of fact based on how the employee's specific tasks correlate to the technical work rather than the employee's job title. Directly engaged duties encompass hands-on experimentation, prototype fabrication, testing, direct technical supervision of SR&ED personnel, technological planning for ongoing SR&ED projects claimed in the tax year (such as planning for the assignment of technological personnel, job priorities, development of technological strategies, and quality of materials used), and specific tasks performed by non-specialized employees—such as operating a machine required for an experiment or feeding raw materials into a machine—when directly supervised by staff with scientific or technological qualifications. Under Subsection 37(1.5) of the ITA, a claimant may also include a limited portion of salary or wages for permissible SR&ED work performed outside Canada by Canadian-resident employees, capped at 10% of the total SR&ED salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada.

Pursuant to Subsection 78(4) of the ITA, any salary, wages, or accrued remuneration (such as vacation pay or bonuses for arm's-length employees) incurred in a taxation year must be paid within 180 days after the end of that taxation year to be eligible in that year. If an accrued remuneration amount remains unpaid on the 180th day following year-end, it cannot be claimed in the year incurred and is instead deemed to be an expenditure incurred in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid (reported on Line 310 of Form T661, though unpaid amounts from a prior year paid in the current tax year are excluded from the salary base for the 55% PPA).

Strict statutory caps and exclusions govern remuneration paid to "specified employees". Under Subsection 248(1) of the ITA, a specified employee of a corporation is an employee who is a "specified shareholder"—defined as a taxpayer who owns, directly or indirectly at any time in the year (including shares owned by persons with whom the employee does not deal at arm's length), 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or of any corporation related to the corporation—or an employee who does not deal at arm's length with the employer (such as a spouse, sibling, or child of a controlling shareholder). For a specified employee, all bonuses and remuneration based on profits are 100% disallowed for SR&ED purposes, and total claimable SR&ED salary or wages are capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under Section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan, prorated for the number of days in the taxation year on which the individual was a specified employee. Furthermore, when calculating the salary base for the 55% PPA under the Proxy Method, the includable salary of each specified employee is further restricted under Subsection 2900(7) of the ITR to the lesser of 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages (across both SR&ED and non-SR&ED duties, excluding bonuses and taxable benefits) and 2.5 times the YMPE, prorated by days.

body.text: A critical statutory trap detailed in Section 6.1.2 of the CRA SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy applies whenever a specified employee performs SR&ED activities for two or more associated corporations (noting that individuals related to a particular corporation, certain partnerships, and certain limited partnerships are deemed to be corporations associated with the particular corporation for this rule). Both the 5 times YMPE expenditure cap and the 2.5 times YMPE PPA cap must be shared among the associated corporations. Crucially, no expenditures may be claimed for the salary or wages of a specified employee of two or more associated corporations unless each associated corporation files with its tax return a completed copy of Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)) accompanied by a certified copy of the resolution of the directors authorizing the agreement (or a signed shareholder confirmation where two corporations are owned exclusively by one sole shareholder) no later than the corporations' respective SR&ED reporting deadlines. If Form T1174 is not filed by the statutory reporting deadline, the entire amount for the salary or wages of the specified employee is statutorily deemed not to be an expenditure on SR&ED.
Materials, Subcontractors, Third-Party Payments, and Cloud Computing

Under Paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the ITR (Traditional Method) and Subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) of the ITA (Proxy Method), a claimant may include 100% of the cost of materials that are either consumed (destroyed or rendered virtually valueless) or transformed (integrated into an experimental prototype, custom rig, or pilot plant where the material ceases to exist in its original form) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Both consumed and transformed materials are 100% deductible in the Section 37 pool and 100% eligible for the Section 127 ITC, subject to the SR&ED Recapture rules under Subsections 127(27) to 127(35) of the ITA if a transformed prototype or material is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use.

When claiming contract expenditures for SR&ED performed in Canada on the claimant's behalf, the ITA enforces a strict distinction between arm's-length contractors and non-arm's-length contractors. Where a claimant engages an arm's-length Canadian contractor to perform SR&ED on its behalf, 100% of the eligible contract payment is included in the Section 37 pool of deductible expenditures, while 80% of the contract expenditure is eligible for the calculation of qualified SR&ED expenditures for the Section 127 ITC. (For contract expenditures made before December 16, 2024, former Subsections 37(14) and 37(15) of the ITA imposed a "capital look-through rule" requiring the payor to reduce its contract claim by any related capital or capital-lease expenditure of the performer, with the performer obligated to notify the claimant in writing within 90 days after calendar year-end; however, following the restoration of capital expenditures after December 15, 2024, performer capital expenditures and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 qualify once again). Conversely, contract payments made to a non-arm's-length contractor can be included in the payor's Section 37 deductible expenditure pool, but they are completely ineligible for an ITC in the hands of the payor. Instead, the non-arm's-length performer must either claim the ITC directly on its own underlying SR&ED costs or execute a transfer agreement under Subsection 127(13) of the ITA to transfer the qualified expenditures to the payor (reported on Line 540 of Form T661). Similarly, third-party payments made to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, approved associations, or approved granting councils for SR&ED in Canada related to a business class of the claimant are 100% deductible in the Section 37 pool and 80% eligible for the Section 127 ITC.

In modern digital technology claims involving artificial intelligence, cloud computing, big data analytics, the Internet of Things (IoT), and blockchain architectures, elastic cloud computing and server hosting expenses represent a major operational expenditure. The SR&ED eligibility of cloud computing costs depends directly on whether the claimant elects the Traditional Method or the Proxy Method. Under the Traditional Method, cloud computing expenses that are strictly segregated from commercial production hosting and are both directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada qualify on Line 360 of Form T661 as "other expenditures" under Paragraph 2900(2)(c) of the ITR, earning both Section 37 deductions and Section 127 ITCs. Under the Proxy Method, because standard cloud utility services are neither physical materials consumed or transformed under Subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) nor SR&ED performed on the claimant's behalf under an SR&ED contract, general cloud hosting costs are treated as overhead captured within the 55% PPA. However, where a claimant enters into a dedicated hardware or bare-metal server lease agreement after December 15, 2024, that constitutes an expenditure for the use of, or the right to use, depreciable capital property, such lease costs are governed by the restored equipment lease rules under the SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy and SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy.
Restored SR&ED Capital Expenditures and Shared-Use Equipment (Post-December 15, 2024)

A cornerstone of the 2024 FES and Budget 2025 legislative package (Royal Assent March 26, 2026) is the full restoration of SR&ED Capital Expenditures, capital equipment lease costs, and Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) for depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024. While capital expenditures and capital property lease costs incurred after 2013 and before December 16, 2024 remain permanently disallowed under Paragraph 37(8)(d) of the ITA, property acquired after December 15, 2024 is eligible under two distinct statutory tracks depending on the intensity of its SR&ED usage.

Under the first track—full SR&ED Capital Expenditures governed by Paragraph 37(1)(b), Subsection 37(1.2), and Subsection 127(9) of the ITA—an expenditure made to acquire new or used depreciable property that becomes available for use after December 15, 2024, qualifies in full (reported on Line 390 of Form T661) if the claimant intended at the time of acquisition to satisfy either of two All or Substantially All (ASA, defined as 90% or more) criteria: either to use the property during all or substantially all (90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life to perform SR&ED in Canada, or to consume all or substantially all (90% or more) of the property's value to perform SR&ED in Canada. Generally, operating time means the time the equipment usually runs or functions; if a claimant's taxation year began before December 16, 2024, the claimant must calculate SR&ED use as a percentage of total operating time for the period after December 15, 2024. Land is a non-depreciable asset and never qualifies, while buildings are excluded as Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Subsection 2900(11) of the ITR. When claimed on Line 390 of Form T661, the full cost of the depreciable property is added to the Section 37 deductible pool (which is deemed to be Capital Cost Allowance [CCA], precluding the claimant from also claiming regular CCA for the same asset on Schedule 8) and qualifies 100% for the SR&ED ITC, where it earns a 40% refundable ITC at the 35% enhanced rate up to the expenditure limit for qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs. Claimants must enter the names of the 10 most expensive SR&ED capital properties acquired after December 15, 2024 per project on Lines 262 and 263 of Part 2 of Form T661, and list the 20 most expensive depreciable properties overall in Box 780 of Part 6.

Similarly, lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, for the use of or right to use equipment qualify if the leased equipment is used ASA (90% or more) in SR&ED (or 50% of the lease cost under the Proxy Method if used primarily, between 50% and 90%, in SR&ED, excluding general purpose office equipment or furniture [GPOEF]); under the Traditional Method, lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 for equipment used in SR&ED less than 90% of the time may be claimed on Line 360 as overhead and other expenditures to the extent incremental to SR&ED.

Under the second track—Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), governed by Paragraph 127(9)(c), Subparagraph 127(9)(a)(iii), Paragraph 127(11.5)(b), and Subsection 127(11.6) of the ITA (which were repealed on February 1, 2017, and reintroduced effective December 15/16, 2024)—equipment that does not meet the 90% ASA test may still earn partial SR&ED ITCs on Line 504 (and Box 788) of Form T661. To qualify as first-term SUE, the property must be new (unused) depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, must not qualify as an ASA SR&ED capital expenditure, must not be Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Subsection 2900(11) of the ITR, must not be general purpose office equipment or furniture (GPOEF), and must be used primarily—meaning more than 50% but less than 90% of its operating time—for SR&ED in Canada during the statutory evaluation periods.

The "first period" for first-term SUE begins at the time the equipment is acquired (and, for eligibility, it must have become available for use after December 15, 2024) and ends at the end of the first taxation year that concludes at least 12 months after that acquisition date (meaning that if equipment is acquired on December 19, 2024, by a corporation with a December 31 year-end, the first period ends on December 31, 2025, because the period from December 19, 2024 to December 31, 2024 is less than 12 months). The "second period" for second-term SUE begins at the time the equipment is acquired and ends at the end of the first taxation year that concludes at least 24 months after that date. If the equipment meets the primary (>50%) SR&ED usage test in the first period, 25% (1/4) of its capital cost (determined without borrowing costs under Section 21 or deemed capital costs under Subsection 13(7.4), and after non-arm's-length adjustments under Subsection 127(11.6)) qualifies for the SR&ED ITC on Line 504 as first-term SUE; if it continues to meet the test in the second period, an additional 25% (1/4) of its capital cost qualifies on Line 504 as second-term SUE, while the asset remains in its normal CCA class on Schedule 8. If SUE property is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, SUE ITC Recapture under Subsection 127(27) claws back the lesser of the SUE ITC obtained or the ITC rate applied to 25% (if only first-term SUE was claimed) or 50% (if both first- and second-term SUE were claimed) of the proceeds of disposition.
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes
Comprehensive Comparison of Provincial and Territorial Regimes

Across Canada, nine provinces (all except Prince Edward Island) and the Yukon territory complement the federal SR&ED program with statutory R&D tax credits. Because every dollar of provincial or territorial R&D tax credit constitutes "government assistance" under Subsection 127(9) of the ITA that reduces federal qualified SR&ED expenditures on Lines 513 and 514 of Form T661 in the year earned, tax practitioners must model the combined federal-provincial interaction simultaneously.

body.text: Deep-Dive Analysis of Key Provincial Architectures
Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and Schedule 500 Gross-Up Mechanics

In Ontario, corporate R&D tax incentives are governed by the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) and administered by the CRA through the T2 Corporation Income Tax Return. The primary incentive for small and medium-sized enterprises is the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC), claimed on Schedule 566, which provides an 8% fully refundable tax credit to qualifying CCPCs on up to $3,000,000 of qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in Ontario (covering 100% of eligible current expenditures and 40% of eligible capital expenditures, phasing out between $500,000 and $800,000 of prior-year taxable income and between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada). Complementing the OITC is the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC), claimed on Schedule 508, which provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit (with a 3-year carryback and 20-year carryforward period) to all corporations with a permanent establishment in Ontario on their eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditure pool after deducting any OITC and Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC, a 20% refundable credit on up to $20,000,000 of eligible research institute contracts claimed on Schedules 568 and 569). Because provincial R&D credits reduce the federal Section 37 pool as government assistance, Ontario provides a dedicated statutory deduction in Part 2 of Schedule 500 (Ontario Corporation Tax Calculation) to reverse the inclusion of Ontario R&D tax credits in Ontario taxable income.
Québec: From Form RD-1029.7 to the Post-March 25, 2025 CRIC Overhaul

Québec administers its corporate income tax regime independently through Revenu Québec under the Taxation Act (Québec), requiring corporate claimants to file a separate Québec corporate income tax return (Form CO-17) and partnerships to file a Partnership Information Return (Form TP-600-V) alongside RL-15 slips for their members. For fiscal periods beginning on or before March 25, 2025, Québec's primary incentive was the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D), claimed on Form RD-1029.7 (which required claimants to enter their Québec Sales Tax [QST] identification number). That legacy regime provided a 100% refundable tax credit at an enhanced rate of up to 30% for SMEs (on up to $3,000,000 of eligible R&D salaries, phasing down to the 14% basic rate as prior-year consolidated worldwide assets increased from $50,000,000 to $75,000,000) and applied strictly to Québec R&D salaries and 50% of arm's-length Québec subcontractor payments, after subtracting a mandatory annual exclusion threshold (seuil d'exclusion) scaling from $50,000 to $225,000.

For fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, however, Québec enacted a transformative structural reform that replaces the fragmented legacy credits and the annual exclusion threshold with the consolidated Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC). As confirmed in Revenu Québec's administrative guidance for corporations and qualified partnerships (Guide TP-600-G-V), the post-March 25, 2025 Québec architecture expands eligible activities beyond core R&D to include pre-commercialization activities carried out in Québec (such as industrial design, engineering, homologation, certification, and pre-production pilot testing). Furthermore, qualifying expenditures under the post-March 25, 2025 regime are broadened to include not only salaries and wages, consideration paid to subcontractors, and payments to eligible research organizations, but also capital expenditures for the acquisition of depreciable property used in R&D or pre-commercialization in Québec. In place of the repealed annual exclusion threshold, access to the enhanced credit rate (30% for corporations; 45% or 20% for corporate members of qualified partnerships depending on whether the partnership operates a mineral resource or oil or gas well, with basic partnership member rates adjusted from 38.75%/28% to 22.5% and from 18.75%/12% to 10%) is governed by a cumulative eligible expense limit, with all eligible expenses incurred on or before March 25, 2025 excluded when computing the balance of that cumulative limit.
Alberta: The Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) and Two-Step Iterative Mechanics

In Alberta, the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG)—administered by Alberta Treasury Board and Finance, Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA) under Division 7 of Part 6 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act and Information Circular IEG-1R5 (updated June 2026) in conjunction with the Ministry of Technology and Innovation—delivers a 100% refundable tax credit for eligible R&D expenditures incurred in Alberta after December 31, 2020. Eligible expenditures for the IEG match federal qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in Alberta, up to a maximum annual expenditure limit of $4,000,000 (shared among associated corporations via an allocation agreement in Column 240 on page 3 of Form AT29 and prorated for short taxation years). To target small and medium-sized enterprises, the $4,000,000 maximum expenditure limit phases out incrementally for corporations (and associated groups) with prior-year taxable capital between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000, becoming nil at $50,000,000 or more.

The IEG provides a two-tier payment calculated on AT1 Schedule 29 (Form AT29) and supported by Form AT4970 (List of Innovation Employment Grant Projects Carried Out in Alberta). First, in Part I of Form AT29 (Line 110), the corporation earns an 8% base payment on the lesser of its eligible Alberta R&D expenditures and its allocated maximum expenditure limit. Second, in Part II of Form AT29 (Line 125), the corporation earns an additional 12% payment (yielding a combined 20% marginal grant rate) on the portion of its eligible Alberta R&D expenditures (up to the $4,000,000 limit) that exceeds the corporation's "base amount". A corporation's base amount is defined as its average eligible Alberta R&D spending over the preceding two taxation years:
Base amount = (eligible Alberta expenditures for the first preceding taxation year + eligible Alberta expenditures for the second preceding taxation year) ÷ 2

For example, if an unassociated corporation claiming the IEG had $0 of eligible Alberta expenditures in Year −2 and $20,000 in Year −1, its base amount is $10,000 (($0 + $20,000) / 2), meaning that on $100,000 of current-year Alberta R&D spending, the first $10,000 earns 8% ($800) and the incremental $90,000 above the base earns 20% ($18,000).

Because the Alberta IEG is calculated from federal qualified SR&ED expenditures (Line 559/557 of federal Form T661) and must simultaneously be deducted as provincial government assistance on Line 513 of federal Form T661, TRA requires a mandatory two-step calculation on Form AT29. In Step 1, the claimant calculates a preliminary IEG on Line 130 of Form AT29 based on federal qualified SR&ED expenditures before deducting the IEG on federal Form T661. Prior to beginning Step 2, the claimant enters that Line 130 preliminary IEG amount onto Line 513 of federal Form T661 as provincial government assistance, which reduces the federal qualified SR&ED expenditures on Line 559/557 of Form T661. In Step 2, the claimant enters the reduced federal qualified SR&ED expenditure total onto Line 003 of Form AT29 to determine the final Net IEG on Line 134 of Form AT29, which is then claimed on Line 129 of the AT1 Return as of the corporation's balance-due day. Moreover, if property included in eligible expenditures for an IEG is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, the Alberta Corporate Tax Act imposes an IEG Recapture addition to Alberta tax payable equal to the lesser of the prorated IEG earned on the original cost of the property or the prorated IEG calculated on the proceeds of disposition:
IEG recapture = the lesser of [(A ÷ B) × (E ÷ F) × C] and [(A₁ ÷ B₁) × (E₁ ÷ F₁) × D] − G

where A (and A₁) represents the IEG received for the claim year, B (and B₁) represents the lesser of eligible expenditures and the $4,000,000 maximum expenditure limit, C represents the cost of the property included in eligible expenditures, D represents the proceeds of disposition, E (and E₁) represents the maximum expenditure limit, F (and F₁) represents the greater of the maximum expenditure limit and total eligible expenditures, and G represents any prior recapture amount under Situation 1.
Governance, Filing Procedures, Audit Protocols, and Statutory Deadlines
Required Forms and Electronic Filing Mandates

Claiming federal and provincial R&D tax incentives in Canada requires filing a coordinated package of prescribed tax forms and schedules with the CRA, Revenu Québec, and Alberta TRA. At the federal level, every claimant must submit Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) alongside Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations) for corporate claimants or Form T2038(IND) for unincorporated individuals and trusts, while recording the Section 37 pool deduction on Line 411 of Schedule T2SCH1. Where specified employees perform SR&ED across associated corporations, each associated corporation must also file Form T1174 and a certified directors' resolution. In Part 8 of Form T661, the claimant and any external claim preparer must certify complete billing and contingency fee details; failure to provide complete or accurate claim preparer information attracts a statutory penalty of $1,000 under Subsection 162(5.1) of the ITA, for which the claimant and the preparer are jointly and severally liable. Furthermore, in Alberta, for taxation years beginning after December 31, 2024, every corporation is legally required to file its AT1 Return and all schedules (including AT1 Schedule 29 and Form AT4970) electronically with TRA using Net File, unless the corporation is an insurance corporation, is a non-resident corporation, or reports in functional currency (or where a tax preparer prepares the return for no payment or prepares 5 or fewer AT1 returns for payment in a calendar year).

body.text: The Strict 18-Month Statutory Filing Deadline

Under Subsections 37(11) and 127(9)(m) of the ITA and the CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy, a taxpayer must file Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 (or Form T2038(IND)) containing the prescribed technical and financial information no later than 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing due date for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred. Because a corporation's T2 income tax return is due 6 months after the end of its taxation year under Paragraph 150(1)(a) of the ITA, a corporation's absolute statutory reporting deadline for filing a complete SR&ED claim is exactly 18 months after the end of its taxation year (while an individual's deadline is 17.5 months after calendar year-end, and a trust's deadline is 12 months plus 90 days after trust year-end).

This 18-month reporting deadline operates as a strict, non-waivable statutory bar. The Minister of National Revenue has no legal discretion under the taxpayer relief provisions of Subsection 220(3.1) of the ITA to accept a late-filed Form T661, Schedule T2SCH31, or Form T1174 after the 18-month period has expired. Any SR&ED project or expenditure line item omitted from Form T661 as of the 18-month deadline is permanently barred from both the Section 37 deductible pool and the Section 127 ITC calculation. Similarly, in Alberta, if AT1 Schedule 29 is submitted after the statutory filing deadline (which mirrors the federal 18-month window), TRA rejects the IEG claim without issuing an assessment—sending an administrative rejection letter instead—though TRA permits the corporation to file a formal Notice of Objection strictly to verify whether the timing of the filing of Schedule 29 was properly considered. Furthermore, under Section 30 of Information Circular IEG-1R1/IEG-1R4/IEG-1R5, TRA will only determine and disburse a qualified corporation's Alberta IEG after the later of the date TRA receives Form AT29 and the date TRA receives official confirmation from the CRA of the assessed amount of the corporation's federal SR&ED expenditures.
CRA Audit Protocols and Budget 2026 Pre-Claim Rulings

Upon receipt of a federal SR&ED claim, the CRA screens the submission through its automated risk-assessment systems, applying advanced data analytics and elements of its SR&ED Large Claim Strategy across claimant cohorts. Claims selected for technical and financial audit are assigned to a coordinated two-person CRA examination team consisting of a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) and a Financial Reviewer (FR). The RTA—an industry-specialized scientist or engineer—evaluates the technical project narratives in Part 2 of Form T661, reviews contemporaneous experimental records, and interviews the claimant's technical leads to verify whether each project satisfies the five Northwest Hydraulic / C.W. Agencies criteria and whether support work was commensurate with the needs of the core experimental development. Concurrently, the FR audits the financial schedules in Parts 3, 4, and 5 of Form T661, reconciling T4 payroll summaries, direct time-tracking records, specified employee Form T1174 allocations, arm's-length vs. non-arm's-length contract invoices, Section 78(4) 180-day payment proof, and post-December 15, 2024 capital asset and SUE operating-time logs.

To provide upfront certainty to businesses before R&D capital is deployed, the CRA administers a pre-claim approval framework, which Budget 2026 substantially elevated by introducing binding upfront CRA rulings before capital is committed, operating under a streamlined "1 project, 1 decision, 1 year" service mandate. Where a post-filing audit results in a proposed downward adjustment, the RTA and FR issue a draft proposal letter providing the claimant 30 days to submit supplementary technical or financial rebuttal evidence and request an administrative review by the CRA SR&ED Field Review Manager. If the CRA proceeds to issue an unfavourable Notice of Assessment or Reassessment, the claimant has 90 days from the date of mailing to file a formal Notice of Objection (Form T400A) with the CRA Appeals Branch, and if the objection is confirmed or remains undecided after 90 days, the claimant may appeal directly to the Tax Court of Canada under either the Informal Procedure or the General Procedure.
Integrated Numerical Simulation: Post-December 15, 2024 Federal and Provincial Claim
Corporate Profile and Input Assumptions

To demonstrate the exact statutory sequence and mathematical interaction of the post-December 15, 2024 federal SR&ED reforms (Royal Assent March 26, 2026) and provincial R&D tax credits, consider "InnovateCan Corp.", an unassociated Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) operating exclusively from a permanent establishment in Toronto, Ontario, with a fiscal and taxation year running from January 1, 2026, to December 31, 2026 (beginning after December 15, 2024). InnovateCan Corp. had prior-year (2025) taxable capital employed in Canada of $12,000,000 and prior-year taxable income of $400,000. Under the pre-December 16, 2024 federal rules, its $12,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital would have triggered a phase-down of its $3,000,000 expenditure limit (reducing it to $2,850,000) because it exceeded the legacy $10,000,000 threshold. Under the post-December 15, 2024 rules, however, because its prior-year taxable capital of $12,000,000 is below the new $15,000,000 phase-out threshold, InnovateCan Corp. qualifies for the full $6,000,000 federal expenditure limit at the 35% enhanced rate, as well as the full $3,000,000 expenditure limit for the 8% Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC). InnovateCan Corp. elects to use the Proxy Method (55% PPA) for its 2026 taxation year.

body.text: Step-by-Step Audit Verification and Tax Credit Computation

In the first audit step, the specified employee caps and the Part 5 Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) are verified. Because the founder owns 25% of the common shares (≥ 10%), the founder is a specified employee; consequently, the founder's $50,000 bonus is 100% disallowed and the founder's PPA salary base is limited to the lesser of the SR&ED portion of base salary (80% × $300,000 = $240,000), 75% of total base salary (75% × $300,000 = $225,000), and 2.5 times the 2026 YMPE (2.5 × $74,600 = $186,500), capping the founder's PPA salary base contribution at $186,500. Combining the arm's-length base salaries of $1,800,000 (excluding the $120,000 arm's-length bonus pursuant to Subsection 2900(4) of the ITR) with the founder's capped salary base of $186,500 yields a total PPA salary base of $1,986,500. Applying the 55% statutory rate produces the Prescribed Proxy Amount:

In the second step, the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures is computed in Part 3 of Form T661. Allowable current SR&ED expenditures on Line 380 comprise $1,920,000 of arm's-length salaries and bonuses, $240,000 of specified employee salary, $585,463 of transformed materials, and 100% of the $500,000 arm's-length subcontractor expenditures, totalling $3,245,463. Adding the $400,000 ASA (95%) capital equipment expenditure on Line 390 brings total allowable SR&ED expenditures on Line 400 (before provincial government assistance) to $3,645,463, while the $200,000 SUE chamber remains in its regular CCA class on Schedule 8.

In the third step, gross qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes are compiled in Part 4 of Form T661 prior to deducting provincial government assistance. Gross current qualified expenditures equal $2,160,000 in total eligible wages ($1,800,000 + $120,000 + $240,000), plus $585,463 in materials, plus $400,000 in arm's-length contracts (80% × $500,000), plus the $1,092,575 PPA, totalling $4,238,038. Gross capital and SUE qualified expenditures equal the $400,000 ASA capital expenditure from Line 390 plus $50,000 for first-term SUE on Line 504 (25% of the $200,000 environmental chamber), totalling $450,000. Thus, total gross qualified SR&ED expenditures equal $4,688,038 ($4,238,038 + $450,000).

In the fourth step, the Ontario provincial R&D tax credits (OITC and ORDTC) are calculated and deducted as provincial government assistance on Lines 513/514 of Form T661. Because InnovateCan Corp.'s gross qualified expenditures ($4,688,038) exceed Ontario's $3,000,000 OITC expenditure limit, the OITC is $240,000 (8% × $3,000,000) on Schedule 566. Next, the eligible Ontario pool for the 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC on Schedule 508 is reduced by the $240,000 OITC to $4,448,038 ($4,688,038 − $240,000), yielding an ORDTC of $155,681 (3.5% × $4,448,038). Total Ontario government assistance deducted on Lines 513/514 of federal Form T661 is therefore $395,681 ($240,000 + $155,681).

In the fifth and final step, deducting the $395,681 of Ontario government assistance reduces net current qualified SR&ED expenditures to $3,842,357 ($4,238,038 − $395,681), while net capital and SUE qualified expenditures remain $450,000, yielding total net federal qualified SR&ED expenditures on Line 559/557 of $4,292,357. Because InnovateCan Corp.'s post-December 15, 2024 federal expenditure limit is $6,000,000, the entire $4,292,357 earns the 35% enhanced rate, for a total federal ITC of $1,502,325: the $1,344,825 ITC on current expenditures (35% × $3,842,357) is 100% refundable, while of the $157,500 ITC on capital and SUE expenditures (35% × $450,000), 40% ($63,000) is refundable in cash and 60% ($94,500) is available to offset Part I tax payable or carry back 3 years / forward 20 years.
Strategic Conclusions and Audit Readiness Framework

The enactment of the post-December 15, 2024 legislative reforms (receiving Royal Assent on March 26, 2026) alongside the Budget 2026 pre-claim ruling reforms represents the most significant expansion of Canadian R&D tax incentives in a generation. By doubling the annual expenditure limit for the 35% enhanced ITC from $3 million to $6 million, elevating the CCPC taxable capital phase-out corridor from $10M–$50M to $15M–$75M, extending the 35% enhanced refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) with three-year average revenues below $75 million, and restoring capital expenditures, equipment lease costs, and Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) acquired after December 15, 2024, Parliament has structurally transformed the economics of capital-intensive and scaling R&D in Canada. At the provincial level, Québec's post-March 25, 2025 CRIC overhaul—which extends refundable credits to pre-commercialization activities and capital property while abolishing the legacy exclusion threshold—and Alberta's 8%/20% Innovation Employment Grant further amplify the after-tax return on Canadian innovation.

To withstand rigorous CRA and provincial audit scrutiny under this expanded statutory landscape, corporate claimants and tax auditors must embed disciplined compliance protocols across both technical engineering operations and tax accounting systems. First, technical narratives in Part 2 of Form T661 must be anchored directly to the five judicial criteria established in Northwest Hydraulic and C.W. Agencies, clearly distinguishing system-level technological uncertainties from routine engineering and preserving dated evidence of hypothesis formulation, experimental protocols, and failed iterations in accordance with Kam-Press and Manning Canning. Second, claimants acquiring depreciable property or leasing specialized equipment after December 15, 2024, must implement machine-level operating logs from the date the equipment becomes available for use to substantiate either the ≥ 90% ASA threshold for Line 390 capital expenditure claims or the >50% to <90% primary usage threshold across the 12-month and 24-month evaluation periods for Line 504 SUE claims. Third, corporate groups employing specified shareholders or non-arm's-length individuals must strictly enforce the 5 times YMPE and 2.5 times YMPE statutory caps, eliminate all specified employee bonuses from SR&ED schedules, ensure all accrued arm's-length SR&ED remuneration is paid within 180 days of year-end under Subsection 78(4), and file Form T1174 with certified directors' resolutions prior to the 18-month reporting deadline. Finally, tax departments must execute iterative federal-provincial government assistance calculations—such as the mandatory two-step calculation on Alberta Form AT29 and federal Line 513—and calendar the 18-month statutory filing deadline as an absolute, non-waivable forfeiture date.
